title: Route-planning MCP: loop / out-and-back / one-way, length range, climb seeking or flat, GPX for Garmin
description:
Why: Eric (2026-10-22) wants to plan rides by talking to Claude: "a 60 km loop from Rathfarnham with hard climbing", "out-and-back to Sally Gap, 50-60 km", "one way to Howth" - and get a GPX he can load on his Garmin. The web planner (epic emq) only does one-way A->B.
High-level design: a Python MCP server (scripts/flow_mcp.py, `mcp` SDK, stdio) that reuses flowplan in-process and talks to the local BRouter. New planning modes built from the existing one-way candidate generator: LOOP (via-points on a ring around the start at several bearings; ring radius iterated until the measured length lands in the requested range), OUT-AND-BACK (route out along several bearings or to a named turnaround at ~half the length; return on the same path by default, optional free return), ONE-WAY (existing). Objectives: flow (expected stops + weighted turns, as today), climb (rank by climb difficulty computed from each route's elevation profile with the climbs.md derivation spec; via-points placed on high ground using the GLO-30 DEM so hard climbs exist among the candidates), flat (least ascent). Length is a range [min,max] km (a single value becomes +-10%). Points come as a place name (Nominatim), raw lat/lon, or a pick-on-map bridge (a tool opens the planner page in pick mode and waits for the click). Output: GPX 1.1 track with elevation, named, written to a chosen folder (Garmin Connect imports it as a course); a short summary table per candidate. The same /api/plan endpoint also powers the web UI's new mode/length/climb controls.
Reuse: flowplan.candidates (BRouter client, multi-point lonlats), scoring (stops), turns (emq.28), ranking, settings (weights, lane_bonus, turn_cost), data/dem GLO-30 tiles + rasterio, scripts/climb_spec_dryrun.py + docs/research/climbs.md (climb points formula), web/index.html.
Out of scope: uploading to Garmin Connect, multi-day routing, surface quality (no open data), regions outside Ireland.
Ambiguities flagged for Eric: (1) out-and-back returns by the same path by default; (2) a one-way ignores the length range (reported, not enforced); (3) 'most difficult climbing' = highest summed climb points (length x gradient^2 style, per climbs.md), not max altitude; (4) the pick-on-map bridge needs the planner page open in a browser on the same machine; (5) BRouter must be running (the MCP can start it when asked).

title: Turn metrics in scoring + ranking on stops plus weighted turns; cards show turns and longest straight stretch
description:
Why: Eric (2026-10-22) wants routes where you ride straight without stopping. The ranking counts expected stops only, so a route with 30 turns and 3 expected stops beats a straight one with 4. Turns must be measured and ranked.
Input: scripts/flowplan/scoring.py (RouteScore, hits with p), scripts/flowplan/explain.py and brouter.py (Candidate.segments from BRouter messages: per-segment lon/lat, dist_m, way_tags, turn_cost), scripts/score_route_stops.py (existing right/left turn heuristic: bearing in/out >= 10 m before/after a junction node, 30..150 deg), scripts/flowplan/ranking.py (rank by expected_stops, guard), scripts/flow_server.py, web/index.html (cards, settings), docs/planner.md.
Steps:
1. flowplan/turns.py: `turn_metrics(geometry, segments=None, stop_hits=None, stop_p_threshold=0.10) -> {turns, turns_per_km, sharp_turns (>60 deg), longest_straight_km, mean_straight_km, turn_points: [{lat, lon, angle_deg}]}` from the route geometry: heading change between the direction of travel ~15 m before and ~15 m after each vertex (projected via REGION_CRS); a turn is a change >= 30 deg; consecutive turn vertices within 25 m count once (S-bends at a junction); if BRouter segments are available, prefer vertices where BRouter charged turn_cost > 0 as the junction indicator and use the geometry for the angle. 'Uninterrupted stretch' = distance between consecutive interruptions, where an interruption is a turn OR a stop hit with p >= stop_p_threshold.
2. RouteScore / stats gain `turns`, `turns_per_km`, `sharp_turns`, `longest_straight_km`, `mean_straight_km`; `turn_points` returned only with debug=1 and drawn in the Explain view as small markers.
3. Ranking objective: `score = expected_stops + turn_weight * turns` with turn_weight default 0.33 (a turn costs a third of a stop) and a server param turn_weight (0..2); keep the 1.3x guard; tie-break by longest_straight_km descending then length. delta_vs_fastest gains a turns delta. Settings slider 'Rank turns as a fraction of a stop' (0..1, default 0.33), hash key tw=; cards show '12 turns (2.1/km), longest straight 2.3 km' and the delta.
4. Tests: synthetic geometries (straight line = 0 turns; a square = 4 turns of 90 deg; an S-bend within 25 m = 1 turn; a gentle 20 deg bend = 0); ranking with turn_weight 0 reproduces the old order; with 0.33 a candidate with many turns drops; longest_straight on a known fixture.
5. planner_eval.py: add turns and longest_straight columns (do not re-run the full eval here; emq.18 will).
6. docs/planner.md: 'Turns and straightness' section with definitions and the ranking formula.
Servers: may be running for the user; restart the flow server if needed and leave it running.
Done: pytest/ruff/ui-check green; live city pair shows turn counts per card and a ranking change at turn_weight 0.33 vs 0 (or an explanation); orchestrator smoke-tests.
notes: Small fix to include (from the emq.27 review): with the default lane_bonus now 0.7, the lanes variant's cap of 0.8 makes 'Add a lanes-favouring route' a no-op; change lanes_variant to use max(0.5, lane_bonus - 0.2) so it is always stronger than the current setting, update its test and the docs line. Servers: BRouter (17777) and the flow server (8081) are RUNNING for the user; this bead changes server code only, so restart the flow server (not BRouter) and leave both RUNNING at the end.

title: Straightness in the router: turn_cost 400, lane_exit_cost via way classifier, cycleway base 1.0, lane_bonus down to 0.5, 'Straight & lanes' default preset
description:
Why: Eric (2026-10-22) says the routes turn far too much; he wants routes where you ride straight without stopping and that significantly favour LONG bike lanes. Today the flow variants dodge signals through residential grids: turncost is a fixed 150 per 90-degree turn, nothing charges for leaving a lane, highway=cycleway carries a 1.3 surcharge from fastbike, and lane_bonus bottoms out at 0.7.
Input: profiles/flow.brf (line ~101 `assign turncost = if junction=roundabout then 0 else 150` in WAY context; line ~106 initialclassifier 1 road / 2 roundabout / 3 ferry; line ~111 way initialcost with cost_rb_entry; the lane_factor/hasbikelane/class_factor block ~272-311 with highway=cycleway base 1.3), scripts/flowplan/{brouter,candidates}.py (validate_params; Variant table; lanes_variant), scripts/flow_server.py (params, cache key, settings echo), web/index.html (Settings panel), docs/planner.md, data/brouter/dist/brouter-1.7.10 (profile developers guide for initialcost/initialclassifier semantics: the NEW way's initialcost is charged when both classifiers are non-zero and differ).
Steps:
1. flow.brf globals (all overridable per request): `turn_cost = 400` (used by the way-context turncost expression in place of 150; roundabout stays 0), `lane_exit_cost = 150` (charged when leaving cycle infrastructure for an ordinary road), `cycleway_base = 1.0` (replaces the 1.3 base for highway=cycleway, so paths are at parity before the discount). lane_bonus range widened to 0.5..1.0 (client validation too).
2. Fragmentation cost: initialclassifier gains class 4 for ways where hasbikelane or highway=cycleway (keep 2 roundabout, 3 ferry; plain roads 1). Way initialcost: ferry 10000; roundabout cost_rb_entry; plain road (classifier 1) `lane_exit_cost`; lane ways (classifier 4) 0. Because BRouter charges the NEW way's initialcost only on a classifier change, this charges lane_exit_cost exactly when a route leaves a lane/path onto a plain road and nothing when entering one or continuing. Document the roundabout interplay (lane -> roundabout -> road charges rb_entry then lane_exit_cost; acceptable). Verify live with a request whose route leaves a cycleway: the InitialCost column in geojson messages shows lane_exit_cost on the first plain-road segment after a lane.
3. Byte-identity is NOT required for this bead (defaults change on purpose). Instead record before/after on the Dublin pair (53.2990,-6.2825 -> 53.2210,-6.2150) and the city pair (53.3330,-6.2600 -> 53.2990,-6.2825): distance, number of turns (heading changes > 30 deg between consecutive segments from geojson messages, via a scratch script), km on lanes/paths, expected stops via flowplan.scoring. Both corridors must still route; data/samples/brouter-*.gpx are regenerated with `scripts/run_brouter.sh route` and committed (< 120 KB each) and docs/research/routing-engines.md gets a one-paragraph note that the samples now reflect the straightness defaults.
4. Server: params turn_cost (0..2000), lane_exit_cost (0..1000), cycleway_base (0.5..2.0) with defaults equal to the profile defaults; applied to flow variants only via profile_params (fastbike untouched so the baseline stays comparable); in the cache key; echoed in settings. Default lane_bonus becomes 0.7 (the 'significantly favour lanes' preset) unless the request says otherwise; document that fastbike is the only variant without the lane preference.
5. UI Settings: a 'Straightness' group: 'Penalise turns' slider (turn_cost 0..1000, default 400), 'Stay on lanes' slider (lane_exit_cost 0..500, default 150), and the existing lane slider now 1.0..0.5 default 0.7; hash keys tc=, le=, lb=; localStorage; Reset-all restores these defaults; preset buttons 'Straight & lanes' (defaults) and 'Plain flow' (turn_cost 150, lane_exit_cost 0, lane_bonus 1.0).
6. Tests: validate_params bounds for the three new params; server echo + cache key; FakeClient sees turn_cost etc. only on flow variants; lanes_variant still works.
7. docs/planner.md: 'Straightness' section (mechanism, defaults, the before/after table, the left/right limitation: BRouter cannot distinguish left from right turns).
Servers: BRouter and the flow server are RUNNING for the user; you MAY restart them (setup + BRouter restart for the profile; flow_server restart) and must leave both RUNNING at the end.
Done: both corridors route; before/after table shows fewer turns and more lane km on both pairs (or an explanation); pytest/ruff/ui-check green; samples regenerated; servers running; orchestrator smoke-tests the sliders.

title: Prefer cycle infrastructure: lane_bonus variable in flow.brf, settings slider, optional flow+lanes variant, km-on-lanes per card
description:
Why: Eric (2026-10-21) wants routes to favour bike lanes when possible. Today profiles/flow.brf (from fastbike) prices highway=cycleway at costfactor 1.3 and uses cycleway* tags only to cap the traffic penalty, so lanes are never favoured.
Steps:
1. profiles/flow.brf: add global 'assign lane_bonus = 1.0' (overridable per request as profile:lane_bonus). In the costfactor expression multiply by lane_bonus when the way is a separate cycle path (highway=cycleway; keep its base 1.3 but let lane_bonus pull it down) OR a road with cycleway/cycleway:left/right/both in lane|track|shared_lane|share_busway|opposite_lane|opposite_track (reuse/extend the existing hascycleway expression into a stricter 'hasbikelane'). With lane_bonus=1.0 routing must be byte-identical to today (verify with scripts/run_brouter.sh route into a scratch dir and diff vs data/samples/brouter-*.gpx ignoring time/creator). Document that cost is per metre, so 0.8 over 10 km equals ~7 signals at the 300 anchor; recommended band 0.7-1.0.
2. flowplan/brouter.py validate_params: lane_bonus finite, 0.5 <= v <= 1.0. flow_server /api/route: param lane_bonus (default 1.0) applied to all flow variants (not fastbike); part of the cache key via the params; echoed in settings. Param lanes_variant=1 adds a fifth variant 'flow_lanes' = flow_scale 1.0 with lane_bonus 0.8 (or the requested lane_bonus if < 1) so the lane-favouring route appears alongside the others; cached like the rest.
3. UI Settings: 'Prefer cycle infrastructure' slider (Off=1.0 .. Strong=0.7, step 0.05, default Off) with the note that it re-routes; a checkbox 'Add a lanes-favouring route' (lanes_variant=1); hash keys lb= and lv=1; localStorage; label 'Flow+lanes' for the new variant.
4. Cards: 'x km on cycle paths, y km on roads with lanes' per route, computed from BRouter per-segment way tags (depends on emq.21 segments; if emq.21 is not yet merged, compute server-side in this bead from the messages the same way and let emq.21 reuse it).
5. Tests: profile byte-identity (live, in the report); validate_params bounds; server echoes lane_bonus and the lanes variant appears when requested (FakeClient); cache key differs when lane_bonus changes.
6. docs/planner.md: section 'Preferring cycle infrastructure' with the mechanism, the per-metre caution and the 8% tagging caveat.
Done: pytest/ruff/ui-check green; live Dublin run shows lane_bonus=0.8 changes the top route or km-on-lanes and the report explains the change; orchestrator smoke-tests the slider.
notes: Ordering: Eric asked for emq.23 BEFORE emq.21, so compute km-on-cycle-infrastructure per route in this bead server-side from BRouter geojson 'messages' (per-segment rows incl. WayTags; the first row is the header; verify column names live) and expose it as stats.cycle_km {path, lane, track}; emq.21 will reuse it. Servers: BRouter (17777) and the flow server (8081) are running for the user; this bead changes flow.brf (needs  to copy it and a BRouter restart) and flow_server.py, so the implementer MAY stop and restart both (make brouter / uv run scripts/flow_server.py --port 8081) and must leave both RUNNING with the new code at the end, and say so. Also apply the emq.20 UI note: bring the route layers to the front after overlays are enabled and after each render.

title: Instant sliders: router costs follow the base weight set only (router=base default); router=table opt-in; blend and per-class sliders re-rank from cache
description:
Why: Eric (2026-10-21) wants instant sliders. Since emq.16 any probability change alters the derived BRouter costs, misses the candidate cache and re-routes (5-8 s). Decision: by default the router's costs are derived from the BASE weight set only (the weights= radio: prior/ireland/combined), ignoring blend and p_<cause> overrides; those still change the scoring/ranking, which is served from the candidate cache instantly. An opt-in keeps the fully consistent behaviour.
Steps:
1. scripts/flow_server.py: new /api/route param router=base|table (default base). base: brouter_costs = StopModel of the base weight set (sets[weights]).brouter_costs(); table: current behaviour (effective model incl. blend/overrides). Echo settings.router and settings.brouter_costs (the costs actually sent). Cache key unchanged (endpoints, scales, costs) so base+slider moves hit the cache. 400 on an invalid router value naming the parameter.
2. Tests (tests/test_server.py, FakeClient call counter): default: a request then the same with p_stop=0 -> second is cached:true and the call count is unchanged; with router=table the same pair misses (count grows); blend_with/blend under base is cached; weights=ireland under base misses once then hits; invalid router -> 400.
3. web/index.html Settings panel: a checkbox 'Router follows sliders (re-routes on every change, 5-8 s)' default off -> router=table when on; hash key r=table only when on; localStorage; a one-line note under the sliders: 'Sliders re-rank the cached candidates instantly; the router searches with the base set's costs' (or the re-route note when the box is on). Status line already shows cached/re-routed. Footer 'router costs' shows the costs actually used. make ui-check.
4. docs/planner.md: update the 'Router and scorer use the same table' subsection and the API section for router=base|table and the latency implications.
5. Live check: start BRouter (make brouter) and the server; Dublin pair: default call, then p_stop=0 -> cached true and total < 200 ms; then router=table&p_stop=0 -> cached false. KILL both servers; pgrep empty.
Done: pytest/ruff green; ui-check ok; live timings in the report; orchestrator smoke-tests the checkbox in the browser.

title: Flow route planner UI: start/end -> handful of highest-flow routes (Ireland first)
description:
Why: epic dhy established that OSM stop causes predict where a bike stops only as probabilities (signals p=0.158, give_way 0.041, stop 0.021, inferred yield 0.016, equal-class 0.021; see docs/research/stop-model-validation.md), and that BRouter can act on node costs (docs/research/routing-engines.md, profiles/flow.brf). Eric now wants a usable local planner: pick a start and an end, see a handful of the highest-flow routes between them. The planner must depend only on open map data plus the LEARNINGS from the ride matching (the per-class probability table), never on Eric's ride files at runtime.

High-level design:
- Candidate generation: BRouter (local RouteServer, scripts/run_brouter.sh) is queried with several profile variants (fastbike baseline + flow profiles retuned to the validated weights at low/normal/high stop-cost scale) x alternativeidx 0..3, giving up to ~16 candidates per OD pair; near-duplicates are removed.
- Scoring: every candidate is re-scored OUTSIDE the router with the full validated model (incl. inferred yield and equal-class, which BRouter cannot express): expected stops = sum over directional arrival events on the route of p(class). Events come from the dhy.10 directional event tables (data/osm/events_<region>.csv, schema way_id,dir,vertex_idx,node_id,cause,amount), compiled once into a self-contained index (event node coord + arrival-from vertex coord) so no PBF is read at request time.
- Ranking: fewest expected stops first, with a distance guard (drop candidates longer than 1.3x the shortest candidate unless fewer than 3 would remain); show top N (default 4).
- UI: FastAPI backend (scripts/flow_server.py) + single-file Leaflet page (web/index.html): click or search (Nominatim) to set start/end, route cards with distance/ascent/expected stops/stops per km/estimated stopped time, routes drawn on the map, expected-stop markers for the selected route, GPX download.
- Region: Ireland first (rd5 tiles present); Berlin as a follow-on task (P3).
Layout: library code in scripts/flowplan/ (package; scripts run from repo root with `uv run scripts/<x>.py`), tests in tests/ (pytest), data products in data/flow/ (gitignored), committed model table in data/model/stop_model.json.
Out of scope: motor-traffic avoidance (TII data useless for minor roads), climb layer, accounts/hosting, mobile.
Ambiguities flagged for Eric: (1) 'handful' = 4 by default, max 6; (2) ranking objective = total expected stops with 1.3x distance guard, stops/km also shown; (3) geocoder = public Nominatim under its 1 req/s policy; (4) Ireland only until the Berlin task.

title: Open-data feasibility study for a custom road-cycling route planner
description:
## Why
Eric has tried Strava, Ride with GPS, Komoot, Garmin Connect and ClimbFinder for planning road-cycling routes and is unhappy with all of them; ClimbFinder's planner is the closest to what he wants. He is considering building his own planner, but the decision hinges on what open data exists.

## What "flow" means (clarified by Eric, 2026-10-20)
**Flow = stretches where a bike rarely has to stop.** The planner should be able to optimise for roads and sequences of roads with few forced stops: traffic signals, stop/give-way junctions, roundabouts, pedestrian crossings, level crossings, turns across traffic, dense junction spacing, and busy roads where joining/crossing forces a yield. Not Strava-heatmap popularity, not surface roughness.

So the central question of this epic is: **can open data predict, per road segment, how often a cyclist will have to stop — and can that prediction be validated against real rides?**

This epic is a **feasibility study, not a build**. Every task produces a note under `docs/research/` following `TEMPLATE.md`, with a hands-on download and a runnable script, and ends in a go/no-go summary.

## Approach
1. **Stop-cause features from OSM** — inventory and coverage of every tag that implies a stop; derive a first "expected stops per km" per way (dhy.10).
2. **Observed stops from ride GPS** — detect actual stop events from Eric's own Garmin/Strava export (and OSM timestamped traces as a fallback), cluster them to OSM nodes (dhy.6).
3. **Validate** — does the OSM feature at a node predict the observed stop probability? Output a per-feature stop-probability table — the seed of a routing cost model (dhy.11).
4. **Routing** — can an open engine take node-level and turn-level stop costs? Hands-on with BRouter (dhy.8).
5. Supporting layers kept from the original plan: road network base (dhy.2), elevation (dhy.3) and climbs (dhy.4) because the ClimbFinder-style climb awareness is still wanted; motor-traffic AADT (dhy.5) demoted to secondary because busy roads cause yield-stops and are a natural second objective.
6. Synthesis (dhy.9).

## Assumptions (flag to Eric if wrong)
- **Primary study region: Ireland** (inferred from .ie domain); light continental spot-check where cheap. Ireland drives on the left: turns across traffic are **right** turns.
- Eric will drop a Garmin Connect or Strava bulk export (FIT/GPX/TCX) into `data/rides/` (gitignored). If absent, dhy.6 proceeds on OSM timestamped traces only and marks the Eric-data section pending.
- Licensing matters: output must be usable in a self-built app (ODbL share-alike etc. recorded per source).

## Descoped
Surface quality beyond OSM (former dhy.7) — closed after clarification. Building the planner — next epic, shaped by dhy.9.

description:
Input: data/dem/glo30_*.tif (Copernicus GLO-30, rasterio already a dependency; tile naming N53_W007 etc; download of missing tiles is out of scope - report the bbox covered), flowplan.plan (via-point generation), flowplan.climbs (climb_score), scripts/elevation_profile.py (existing DEM sampling code to reuse).

Steps: 1) Dem over all tiles found in data/dem; `coverage()` returns the union bbox; sampling outside -> None. 2) climb_via_points: sample a polar grid around the start (n headings x 3 radii between 0.5r and 1.2r); score each point = elevation gain from the start elevation (clamped >= 0) + 0.5 x local relief (max - min of 4 neighbours at 500 m); return the top n sorted by score. 3) plan.py objective='climb' (loops and out-and-backs): instead of evenly spaced headings, build loops through the top-scoring via-points (pairs/triples that are >= 60 degrees apart in bearing) and out-and-backs toward the top via-points; still enforce the length range by radius iteration; objective='flat': prefer via-points with the LOWEST relief score (the same machinery inverted). 4) Document the heuristic honestly: it finds hills near the start, not catalogued climbs; a climb catalogue is a separate future step (reference climbs.md open questions).

title: flowplan.plan: loop and out-and-back candidate generation with length-range targeting (via-point rings, radius iteration)
description:
Input: flowplan.candidates (BRouterClient.route accepts a list of points; DEFAULT_VARIANTS; dedupe; profile_params), flowplan.scoring REGION_CRS.
Output: scripts/flowplan/plan.py with `plan_candidates(client, mode, start, end=None, length_km=(min,max), bearings=8, variants=DEFAULT_VARIANTS, alts=(0,), max_calls=48, profile_params=None, region='ireland', return_mode='same'|'free', progress=None) -> PlanResult(kept, dropped, skipped, calls, notes)`; tests/test_plan.py with a FakeClient that returns synthetic geometries of controllable length.
Steps: 1) LOOP: for each of `bearings` headings theta, via-points at theta, theta+120, theta+240 degrees on a ring of radius r (projected CRS), start -> v1 -> v2 -> v3 -> start; initial r = target/(2*pi) * 1.15 (road detour factor, documented); route, measure length; adjust r by the ratio target/measured (max 3 iterations per heading, stop when inside [min,max]); keep candidates inside the range; also try 2-via (theta, theta+180 at r') variants if the 3-via loop fails to route. 2) OUT-AND-BACK: if `end` given, route start->end and set the turnaround there (length = 2x); else for each heading route to a point at distance d = target/2 * 1.15 along theta, adjust d like r; return_mode 'same' = reverse the out geometry (no second BRouter call; GPX is out + reversed); 'free' = a second BRouter call end->start with the via-point list reversed and alternativeidx 1 so the return differs (dedupe against the out path: if > 70% overlap, fall back to 'same'). 3) ONE-WAY: delegate to candidates.generate; length range is reported in notes, not enforced. 4) Budget: never exceed max_calls BRouter requests; return what was found with a note; concurrency through the existing ThreadPoolExecutor pattern (max_workers 4). 5) Dedupe loops with the existing 20 m/90% rule applied to the full loop geometry; also drop loops whose out and back legs overlap > 60% (they are out-and-backs in disguise) unless mode is out-and-back. 6) Each candidate records mode, heading, via-points, r/d, iterations, length_km. 7) Tests: FakeClient geometry generator; the radius iteration converges into the range within 3 iterations for a linear fake; out-and-back 'same' geometry is palindromic; max_calls respected; one-way passthrough.
Done: pytest green; ruff clean; a live smoke in the report: loop 40-50 km from 53.2990,-6.2825 with 8 bearings -> at least 3 kept candidates with lengths inside the range and the BRouter call count (needs BRouter running: `make brouter`; leave servers as you found them).

title: UI settings panel: weight set, blend with Irish rides, per-class sliders with set ticks, guard, scales; instant re-rank; hash persistence
description:
Why: Eric wants to adjust the stop heuristics from the UI, including toward his ride data.
Input: web/index.html, the emq.15 API (/api/model; /api/route params weights, blend_with, blend, p_<cause>, guard, scales, n, refresh; response `settings`, `model`, `cached`), emq.16 (router follows the table).
Steps:
1. A collapsible 'Settings' section in the side panel (collapsed by default; a badge shows the active weight set and 'custom' when any override is set).
2. Weight set: three radio buttons Prior (literature) / My Irish rides / Pooled (Ireland+Berlin), with a one-line description each taken from /api/model notes; a 'Blend with my Irish rides' slider 0-100% (shown when the base set is not ireland).
3. Per-class sliders for the seven causes (0-1, step 0.005; label with the human name: Traffic signals, Signalled crossing, Stop sign, Give way, Minor-road yield (inferred), Equal-priority junction, Roundabout entry), initialised from the effective set/blend; each slider shows three tick marks for prior/ireland/combined values with tooltips (p and passes/notes); a 'reset to set' link per slider and a global 'Reset'. Changing a slider marks it as an override (sent as p_<cause>).
4. Routing settings: distance guard slider 1.0-2.0 (and 'off'), flow-scale variants as three editable numbers (defaults 0.5/1/2), route count.
5. Behaviour: any model/guard change re-requests /api/route immediately (debounced 250 ms); because candidates are cached server-side this is instant unless scales changed; show 'cached' vs 'routed' and timing in the status line. Settings serialise into the URL hash (short keys) and localStorage; hash wins on load.
6. Each route card shows expected stops under the active table; add a small 'under your Irish rides this would be X' secondary line only when the active set is not ireland (one extra request with weights=ireland is NOT needed: compute client-side from hits[].cause and the ireland p's from /api/model; hits are already in the response).
7. Verification: make ui-check; curl-based field checklist against /api/model and /api/route with settings; the orchestrator does the browser smoke test.
Done: ui-check ok; field checklist complete; no console errors in the smoke test; settings round-trip through the hash.
notes: API facts from emq.15/16: /api/model -> {default_weight_set, precedence, weight_sets{name{cause{p,p_lo,p_hi,mean_stop_s,note}}}, midway_background_p}. /api/route params: weights, blend_with+blend (must be given together), p_<cause> (seven causes: signal, xing_signal, stop, give_way, yield_infer, yield_equal, rb_entry), guard (0=off..3), scales (comma floats; fastbike always included; 0.5,1,2 default), n (1-6), refresh=1. Response adds settings{weights,blend_with,blend,overrides,guard,scales,n,brouter_costs}, model{cause:p}, cached (bool), weight_set (effective name e.g. 'prior+custom', 'blend(prior,ireland,0.50)'). Changing weights/blend/p_* changes BRouter costs so it RE-ROUTES (cache miss, 5-8 s) unless the derived costs are unchanged; guard and n changes are instant (cache hit). UI should say which happened ('re-routed' vs 'cached'). Edge: p_signal=0 keeps cost_signal at the anchor; show a hint. Variant labels: fastbike Fastest, flow_lo Flow-light, flow Flow, flow_hi Flow-heavy, flow_<x> 'Flow x<x>'.

title: Router follows the table: flow.brf node costs as overridable variables; server derives BRouter costs from the active p-table
description:
Why: today BRouter searches with fixed node costs (signals 300, crossing 300, give_way 80, stop 60, mini-roundabout 80, roundabout entry 150) while the scorer ranks with whatever p-table the user picks. When Eric lowers stop signs or roundabouts in the settings, the router should search accordingly.
Input: profiles/flow.brf (node-context initialcost block, flow_scale multiplier; way-context roundabout entry 150), scripts/run_brouter.sh, scripts/flowplan/{brouter,candidates}.py (Variant params -> profile:<var>=<value>), data/model/stop_model.json (p, mean_stop_s per class).
Steps:
1. flow.brf: replace the literal node costs with global `assign` variables cost_signal=300, cost_xing_signal=300, cost_give_way=80, cost_stop=60, cost_mini_rb=80, cost_rb_entry=150 (the way-context roundabout workaround uses cost_rb_entry), each still multiplied by flow_scale; defaults unchanged so routes are byte-identical to today (verify: re-route the Dublin and Wicklow pairs and diff against data/samples/brouter-*.gpx ignoring time/creator lines).
2. flowplan/stop_model.py: `StopModel.brouter_costs(anchor=300) -> dict` = anchor x (p x mean_stop_s)/(p_signal x mean_stop_s_signal) per class, mapped to the six cost_* variables (xing_signal -> cost_xing_signal; give_way; stop; rb_entry -> both cost_mini_rb and cost_rb_entry), clamped to [0, 1000] and rounded to int; document that this is the same formula as the validation note's weight_300.
3. candidates.generate: accept `profile_params: dict` merged into every flow variant's params (fastbike untouched). flow_server: pass model.brouter_costs() for the effective model of the request (after weights/blend/overrides). The candidate cache key (emq.15) must include the cost dict (so changed costs re-route; unchanged costs hit the cache).
4. Validation on the server side: each cost finite, 0..1000.
5. Tests: brouter_costs for the prior set and for an override p_stop=0 (cost_stop 0); generate() passes profile_params through (FakeClient records params); flow.brf still loads (live check in the report) and default-cost routes are unchanged.
6. docs/planner.md: one paragraph 'router and scorer use the same table'.
Done: pytest/ruff green; byte-identical default routes; live run shows p_stop=0 changes the Dublin candidate set or the report explains why not; no servers left running.
notes: Carry-overs from the emq.15 review to fix in passing: ranking.rank docstring should state guard<=0 disables the guard; flow_server reloads non-default weight sets from disk per request (load the three sets once at startup into a dict); /api/model should serve from the app's loaded model path, not always the default file.

title: API: per-request model settings (weights, blend, per-class p, guard, scales) + /api/model + candidate cache for instant re-rank
description:
Why: Eric (2026-10-21) wants to adjust the stop heuristics from the UI, including toward his own ride data. The server must accept per-request model settings and re-rank instantly without re-routing.
Input: scripts/flow_server.py, scripts/flowplan/{stop_model,scoring,ranking,candidates}.py, data/model/stop_model.json (weight_sets combined/ireland/prior, precedence, mean_stop_s).
Output: API extensions + candidate cache + tests.
Steps:
1. stop_model.py: add `StopModel.with_overrides(p: dict[cause,float]) -> StopModel` (copy; validates 0<=p<=1; unknown cause -> KeyError listing causes) and `blend(a: StopModel, b: StopModel, alpha: float) -> StopModel` (p and mean_stop_s linear per class; alpha in [0,1]; weight_set name f"blend({a.weight_set},{b.weight_set},{alpha:.2f})"). Tests.
2. GET /api/model -> {default_weight_set, precedence, weight_sets: {name: {cause: {p, p_lo, p_hi, mean_stop_s, note}}}, midway_background_p} straight from the JSON (so the UI can draw ticks and tooltips).
3. GET /api/route new optional query params: weights=prior|ireland|combined (default server default), blend_with=<set>&blend=<alpha> (optional second set + alpha), p_<cause>=<float> for any of the seven causes (per-class override applied after blend), guard (0.0=off .. 3.0, default 1.3), scales=<comma floats> (flow_scale variants, default 0.5,1,2; each validated via the client's flow_scale rule; fastbike always included), n. Validation errors -> 400 with a message naming the parameter. The response echoes the effective settings under `settings` and the effective per-class p under `model` so the UI can confirm what was applied.
4. Candidate cache: an in-process LRU (size 32) keyed by (round(from,5), round(to,5), scales tuple) holding (kept, dropped, skipped, brouter_ms). A route request with a cache hit skips BRouter entirely and reports timings_ms.brouter = 0 and `cached: true`. Scoring+ranking always re-run with the request's model. Also GET /api/route?...&refresh=1 bypasses the cache.
5. Tests (tests/test_server.py with the FakeClient): /api/model shape; weights=ireland changes expected_stops vs default; p_signal=0 lowers the signal class to zero expected; a blend with alpha 0.5 gives p halfway; bad p -> 400; second identical request is cached (FakeClient call count does not grow) and refresh=1 re-calls; guard=0 disables the guard.
6. docs/planner.md API section updated with the new params and the cache behaviour.
Done: pytest green, ruff clean, manual curl showing a cached second call under 200 ms total; no servers left running.

title: flow_server uses 4 BRouter client threads but run_brouter.sh serves with 2 server threads: long routes get 'thread-priority-watchdog' kills (10-13 of 16 candidates skipped on 20-50 km pairs, found in emq.10); planner_eval uses --workers 2
description: Found in emq.10: scripts/run_brouter.sh serve starts BRouter RouteServer with 2 threads (last arg) while flowplan.candidates.generate() defaults to max_workers=4 and flow_server.py uses that default; on 20-50 km pairs BRouter kills queued requests with 'thread-priority-watchdog' and 10-13 of 16 candidates are silently skipped (they appear in the API's skipped[] list but the UI shows fewer/worse routes). Steps: 1) Decide and implement ONE consistent fix: either start the server with 4 threads in run_brouter.sh (check BRouter RouteServer's thread arg semantics and whether the watchdog is about queue wait time: look in the dist docs and test empirically on the longest pair swords_bray 53.4597,-6.2181 -> 53.2028,-6.0983 with 4 workers) OR set DEFAULT max_workers=2 in candidates.generate and flow_server (and planner_eval already uses 2). Prefer the option that gives zero skipped on all 10 pairs in data/samples/planner_od_pairs.csv with the lowest wall time; record both timings in docs/planner.md (Known limits / latency paragraph). 2) Make flow_server log a WARNING whenever skipped is non-empty, including the error string. 3) Add a test in tests/test_server.py that a skipped entry is surfaced in the JSON. 4) Re-run scripts/planner_eval.py with the chosen defaults and confirm skipped=0 on all rows; if the CSVs change, regenerate data/samples/planner_eval*.csv and the table in docs/planner.md. Done: zero skipped on all 10 pairs with the default settings of flow_server; pytest/ruff green; docs updated; no servers left running.
notes: From the emq.10 review: the watchdog kill is NOT logged by BRouter; it only appears in the HTTP 400 body 'operation killed by thread-priority-watchdog after 0/1 seconds'. With 4 workers 67/160 requests were skipped across the 10 pairs and lucan_dalkey lost its fastbike alt0 request. Also in passing: planner_eval.py 'no fastbike alt0 candidate' error should include the skip reason; its docstring says alt0 is 'always kept' which only holds when the request succeeds. Check data/samples/planner_od_pairs.csv rows 6 and 8: Sally Gap crossroads is near 53.137,-6.314 (file has 53.1013,-6.3010, ~4 km off) and Wicklow Gap summit may be 2-3 km north of 53.012,-6.399; correct coordinates or names, re-run the eval if you change them, and regenerate the CSVs/table.

description:
Why: Eric (2026-10-21) wants the planner to depend as little as possible on his own rides. The validated probability table (data/model/stop_model.json) is pooled Ireland+Berlin and Berlin-weighted; the regions disagree on give_way (Ireland weight 152-217 vs Berlin 17-23 on the signals=300 scale). Smart Dublin / Dublin City Council See.Sense cycling data: find the dataset(s) on data.smartdublin.ie and data.gov.ie (search 'See.Sense', 'cycling', 'braking'), download, list the columns and the licence, and state whether any field is a stop, dwell, braking or speed-drop metric per road segment or junction, with coverage (how many segments, which years). 2. DCC SCATS: search data.gov.ie / Smart Dublin for SCATS cycle time, phase, green split, 'SCATS detector volumes', 'traffic signal timing'. Download what exists, list columns and licence. State whether red fraction per approach can be derived. Acceptance: same as 1.

Do NOT build anything; assess in <= 3 sentences whether bus dwell away from stops could proxy signal red time, and the main confounders. Acceptance: licence + update frequency stated.

Literature / structural priors: find at least three citable sources with numbers for (a) cyclist stop probability or delay at signalised intersections as a function of cycle length/green share, (b) yield/stop probability for cyclists at give-way or uncontrolled junctions by major-road class or volume, (c) any Irish or UK cyclist junction delay study. For each: citation, the number, and the conditions. Done-criteria: the note exists with all five TEMPLATE sections; steps 1 and 2 have hands-on evidence (downloaded file sizes/columns) or an explicit 'not published' with the URLs tried; step 5 has >= 3 sources and the three-column comparison table; verdict present; nothing committed in data/ above 1 MB; ruff/pytest unaffected.

title: flow_server.py: FastAPI /api/route with ranking (fewest expected stops, 1.3x distance guard)
description:
Input: flowplan.scoring (FlowIndex, score), flowplan.candidates (generate), flowplan.stop_model, BRouter client.
Output: scripts/flow_server.py (FastAPI), scripts/flowplan/ranking.py, tests/test_ranking.py, pyproject deps fastapi + uvicorn.

Steps:
1. `uv add fastapi uvicorn[standard]`. flow_server.py: `uv run scripts/flow_server.py [--region ireland] [--port 8081] [--brouter http://localhost:17777]`; on startup loads StopModel and FlowIndex once (log load time) and checks BRouter health (log a warning, do not exit, if down).
2. ranking.py: `rank(scored: list[ScoredCandidate], n=4, guard=1.3, min_keep=3) -> list[ScoredCandidate]`: sort by expected_stops ascending, tie-break by length; drop candidates with length > guard x shortest length unless that would leave fewer than min_keep; return top n. Also compute for each returned candidate `delta_vs_fastest`: stops and km relative to the fastbike alt-0 candidate (if present).
3. API: `GET /api/health` -> {brouter: bool, region, index_rows, model_version, bbox}; `GET /api/route?from=lat,lon&to=lat,lon&n=4` -> JSON {query, routes: [{rank, id, profile, alt, geometry: GeoJSON LineString, stats: {distance_km, ascent_m, brouter_time_s, expected_stops, stops_per_km, expected_stop_s, by_class}, delta_vs_fastest, hits: [{lat,lon,cause,p}]}], candidates_total, candidates_deduped, timings_ms}. Validation: lat/lon parse, both points inside the region bbox (ireland: lon -10.7..-5.4, lat 51.3..55.5) else 400 with a message; n clamped to 1..6; BRouter unavailable -> 503 with the run_brouter.sh hint.

title: flowplan.brouter + candidates: BRouter client, profiles x alternatives, near-duplicate removal
description:
Input: BRouter RouteServer on localhost:17777 (scripts/run_brouter.sh serve), profiles fastbike, flow_lo, flow, flow_hi (bead: retune profiles), BRouter URL API: /brouter?lonlats=lon,lat|lon,lat&profile=NAME&alternativeidx=0..3&format=geojson.
Output: scripts/flowplan/brouter.py, scripts/flowplan/candidates.py, tests/test_candidates.py with recorded fixtures in tests/fixtures/.

Steps:
1. brouter.py: `BRouterClient(base_url='http://localhost:17777', timeout_s=20)`; `route(points, profile, alternativeidx) -> Candidate | None`; `health() -> bool` (a tiny known-good Dublin request). Parse format=geojson: geometry coordinates (lon, lat, ele), properties track-length (m), filtered ascend (m), total-time (s), plus 'cost'. BRouter signals failure with HTTP 200 and a text body (e.g. 'no track found', or an 'Error' line) or non-200: return None and record the message in `last_error`. Points outside loaded segments produce an error too; surface it as a clean message.
2. candidates.py: `generate(client, start, end, profiles=('fastbike','flow_lo','flow','flow_hi'), alts=(0,1,2,3), max_workers=4) -> list[Candidate]` running requests concurrently (ThreadPoolExecutor; BRouter server was started with 2 threads so cap at 4 in flight). Each Candidate carries profile, alt, geometry (list of (lon,lat)), length_m, ascent_m, time_s.
3. Dedupe: project to the region CRS (reuse the CRS table from flowplan.scoring), build a 20 m buffer of each kept candidate; a new candidate is a duplicate if >= 90% of its length lies inside an already-kept candidate's buffer. Keep order: fastbike alt 0 first, then by profile order, then alt. Record `duplicate_of` on dropped ones (return both kept and dropped lists for debugging).
4. Fixtures: record the raw geojson responses for the Dublin pair (-6.2825,53.2990 -> -6.2150,53.2210; via -6.2110,53.2560 is NOT used here, two points only) for all 16 combinations into tests/fixtures/brouter_dublin_*.json (each < 300 KB; if larger, record only 8 and say so). tests use a fake client that replays fixtures.
5. tests: parse one fixture (length within 1% of track-length property); dedupe keeps at least 3 and at most 16 candidates on the fixtures; an error body yields None with last_error set.
Edge cases: start == end; BRouter down (connection refused -> raise BRouterUnavailable with a message pointing at run_brouter.sh serve); a profile missing on the server (text error) -> skip that profile and continue.
Done-criteria: pytest green including fixture tests; a live run script step in the report: how many of 16 succeeded, how many kept after dedupe, with their profile/alt/length; ruff clean; no server left running.

title: flowplan.scoring: score any route geometry with the validated model; parity with score_route_stops.py
description:
Input: data/flow/ireland.index.csv (bead: build_flow_index), data/model/stop_model.json (bead: stop model table), scripts/score_route_stops.py (reference implementation; do not modify), the four committed sample routes data/samples/brouter-{dublin,wicklow}-{baseline,flow}.gpx.
Output: scripts/flowplan/scoring.py, tests/test_scoring.py, scripts/flow_score.py (thin CLI).

Steps:
1. scoring.py: `class FlowIndex` built from an index csv: projects event-node and from-node coordinates to EPSG:2157 (parametrise the CRS per region: ireland -> EPSG:2157, berlin -> EPSG:25833), builds a shapely STRtree over event nodes; `FlowIndex.load(region)` reads data/flow/<region>.index.csv; load time must be < 10 s for Ireland (report it).
2. `score(points: list[(lon,lat)], model: StopModel, snap_m=5.0) -> RouteScore` where RouteScore has: distance_km (haversine over points), expected_stops (float), expected_stop_s, stops_per_km, by_class {cause: (events_hit, expected)}, hits = list of {lat, lon, node_id, cause, p, dist_along_km}, and diagnostics {points, matched_nodes}. Matching rule: for each consecutive pair (A,B) of route points, candidate events are index rows whose event node is within snap_m of B; an event matches if its from-node is within snap_m of A, OR the event has no from-node and no other event at that node matched. Apply the precedence/dedup rule from stop_model.py per (node_id, way_id, dir). Do NOT use the `amount` column for probability.
3. Parity check against the reference: write scripts/flow_score.py (`uv run scripts/flow_score.py ROUTE.gpx ... [--region ireland]`) printing a markdown table (distance_km, expected_stops, stops_per_km, per-class event counts). Run it AND `uv run scripts/score_route_stops.py` (with --events data/osm/events_ireland.csv) on the four sample GPX files. Per-class EVENT COUNTS must match the reference exactly for signal, xing_signal, stop, give_way, rb_entry; yield_infer and yield_equal counts must match within 2 events per route (the reference counts amounts, so compare event counts, not amounts; if the reference only prints amounts, divide yield_equal by 0.5). Put both tables in the report and in the module docstring.
4. tests/test_scoring.py: synthetic 3-node fixture index (one signal node with from-node, one stop node reached from the wrong direction) asserting the directional rule: approaching from the matching side scores p(signal), the wrong-direction stop sign scores 0; plus a test that distance_km of a 1 km straight line is within 1%.
Edge cases: route points fewer than 2 -> empty score; points outside the region -> zero hits with diagnostics.matched_nodes == 0 (not an exception); duplicate consecutive points.
Done-criteria: parity tables as specified; pytest green; ruff clean; FlowIndex load time reported.

title: build_flow_index.py: compile directional stop events into a self-contained per-region index (no PBF at request time)
description:
Input: data/osm/events_ireland.csv (469,980 rows; schema way_id,dir,vertex_idx,node_id,cause,amount; dir in {fwd,bwd}; 'arriving on way_id in direction dir at vertex vertex_idx (= node_id)'), data/osm/ireland.osm.pbf, data/osm/event_node_coords_ireland.csv (check its schema first; use it only if it has node_id,lat,lon).
Output: scripts/build_flow_index.py and data/flow/ireland.index.csv (gitignored; add `data/flow/` to .gitignore).

Purpose: a self-contained per-region index so the request-time scorer never opens a PBF. For each event we need the coordinate of the event node AND the coordinate of the vertex the rider arrives FROM (previous vertex on way_id in direction dir), so a route can be matched by consecutive point pairs.

Steps:
1. Script CLI: `uv run scripts/build_flow_index.py --region ireland` (also accepts --pbf, --events, --out overrides; defaults derived from region). Acceptance: --help documents the output schema.
2. Read the events csv; collect the set of needed way_ids. Single pyosmium pass over the PBF with locations: for each needed way, record its node id sequence. Memory note: only ~tens of thousands of ways are needed; do not store all ways.
3. For each event (way_id, dir, vertex_idx, node_id, cause, amount): verify way.nodes[vertex_idx] == node_id (if not, try to locate node_id in the way; if still absent, count as `dropped_missing_vertex`). Arrival-from vertex: fwd -> index vertex_idx-1, bwd -> vertex_idx+1; if out of range (event at the way's first vertex in fwd direction etc.) set from_lat/from_lon empty and count `no_from_vertex` (these are still kept; the scorer handles them by node-only match).
4. Write data/flow/<region>.index.csv with header: node_id,lat,lon,from_node_id,from_lat,from_lon,way_id,dir,cause,amount. Coordinates to 7 decimals.
5. Print a summary to stderr: events in, rows out, dropped_missing_vertex, no_from_vertex, per-cause counts; and exit non-zero if rows out < 95% of events in.
6. Add a Makefile target `flow-index` (REGION ?= ireland) that runs the script.
Edge cases: events csv may have a trailing header-only line; ways deleted from the PBF since the events were generated (count and drop); duplicate (node_id, way_id, dir) rows with different causes (keep all; the scorer applies precedence).
Done-criteria: `make flow-index` produces data/flow/ireland.index.csv with >= 95% of events retained; rows have non-empty lat/lon; `head` of the file shows plausible Irish coordinates (lat 51-55.5, lon -10.7 to -5.4); the summary counts are copied into the implementer report; `uvx ruff check scripts/` clean; `uv run pytest -q` still passes.

description:
## Why
Every bead so far produces tables and CSVs. Eric asked to see the results on a map, and the validation (dhy.11) is far easier to judge visually: which junctions in his own riding does the OSM stop model get wrong? This bead builds a self-contained Leaflet viewer over the sample files that already exist. No server, no build step.

## Inputs (all already in the repo under data/samples/ unless noted)
- `observed_stops_eric.csv`, `observed_stops_eric_berlin.csv` — node_id, lat, lon, passes, stops, probability, mean_stop_s
- `stops_per_km_wicklow.csv`, `stops_per_km_berlin.csv` — per-way expected stops/km (way_id, name, highway, length_km, stops_fwd/bwd, stops_per_km_fwd/bwd). These have NO geometry; see step 2.
- `brouter-{wicklow,dublin}-{baseline,flow}.gpx` — routes from dhy.8
- From dhy.11 (must exist before this bead runs): `stop_model_unexplained_{ireland,berlin}.csv` (unit lat/lon, passes, stops, class, label) and per-unit class output if dhy.11 wrote one; if dhy.11 only wrote per-class aggregates, derive per-unit class by re-running its classification function (import from `scripts/validate_stop_model.py`) and write `data/samples/stop_units_{ireland,berlin}.geojson`.

## Steps
1. `scripts/build_map_data.py`: converts the inputs into small GeoJSON files under `docs/map/data/`: (a) `stops_<region>.geojson` points with passes, stops, probability, mean_stop_s, class (from dhy.11 units where available, else "unclassified"); (b) `ways_<region>.geojson` LineStrings for the ways in the stops/km CSVs, with stops_per_km (mean of fwd/bwd), highway, name — geometry read from the PBF with one pyosmium pass restricted to those way ids (Ireland: `data/osm/ireland.osm.pbf`, Berlin: `data/osm/brandenburg.osm.pbf`); (c) `routes.geojson` from the four GPX files with a `profile` and `pair` property; (d) `unexplained_<region>.geojson` from dhy.11. Keep every GeoJSON ≤ 2 MB (round coords to 5 dp; drop ways < 50 m; if still too big, keep only ways with ≥ 2 passes in the observed data). Acceptance: files present, sizes logged by the script.
2. `docs/map/index.html`: single-file Leaflet page (Leaflet from a CDN, pinned version, e.g. 1.9.4; no other dependencies; inline CSS/JS). Base layer OpenStreetMap tiles with attribution. Layer control with: ways coloured by stops/km on a fixed 5-step scale (0–0.2 green … > 3 red, legend shown); observed stop nodes as circles sized by log(passes), coloured by probability (0 grey → 1 red), popup with passes/stops/p/mean seconds/class; routes (baseline dashed, flow solid, one colour per pair); unexplained units as distinct markers with the manual label in the popup. title: Fix stop-feature attribution leftovers: behind-fallback, way-boundary walk, unqualified-sign direction
description:
## Why
Reviewer of dhy.10 measured that approach-node attribution in `scripts/osm_stop_features.py` (rule 1b) correctly suppresses inference for 89.9% of the 69,029 explicit approach events. The remaining ~9% still double-count or suppress the wrong approach. Small in aggregate (≈ a tenth of the before/after shift already documented) but dhy.11 will fit per-feature stop probabilities on these per-way numbers, so fix first.

## Leftovers to fix (all in `scripts/osm_stop_features.py`, attribution block ≈ lines 298-349)
1. **"Behind" fallback is ineffective** (≈342-344): it keys (junction, way, direction) on a junction the cyclist has already passed, so it matches nothing (3,788 events) or the opposite approach (692 events). Fix: remove the behind fallback, or re-aim it so it suppresses the approach *into* that junction from the sign's side only when the sign's direction points at it; otherwise count as standalone. Acceptance: the fallback's "key never matches" count is 0 in the attribution summary.
2. **Walk stops at way boundaries** (≈328): 1,975 events end at a node where the way merely continues as another way id, so the real junction further on is still double-counted. Fix: continue the walk across same-class continuation nodes (node shared by exactly 2 ways, same class, end vertex of both) until the 60 m cap or a junction. Acceptance: "walk ended at continuation node" count reported and < 200.
3. **Unqualified signs walked both ways** (≈316): where a junction lies within 60 m on the side the sign does not face, a real yield is suppressed (5,622 both-direction landings). Fix: for unqualified `highway=stop|give_way` nodes, walk only toward the nearer junction (ahead by way geometry in each direction; pick the closer one); keep both directions only for unqualified `traffic_signals` on two-way ways (signals usually control both). Acceptance: the number of (junction, way, dir) keys suppressed by unqualified stop/give_way nodes drops and is reported.
4. Update the attribution summary printed by `--report` so it lists: attributed ahead · attributed via continuation · standalone · suppressed keys. Update note rule 1b (`docs/research/osm-stop-features.md:36`) to describe exactly what is implemented and to disclose any residual double counting with its measured share.
5. Rerun on Ireland; regenerate `data/samples/osm_stop_features_ireland.md`, `data/samples/stops_per_km_wicklow.csv` (keep < 1 MB), and refresh every number in the note (headline counts unchanged; per-class median/p90, cause breakdown, top-20 stretches, before/after section). Wall time must stay < 10 min.

## Done when
Script changes in place; the reviewer's scratch measure (share of explicit approach events whose junction approach is suppressed) is ≥ 97%; note updated with the new numbers and an honest residual-error statement; ruff clean.
close_reason: Reviewer PASS: residual double counting 0.04% of approach events; disclosure sentence added in-commit

title: Validate: do OSM stop-cause features predict observed stop probability? Per-feature stop-probability table
description:
## Question
Do the OSM stop-cause features (dhy.10) predict the observed stop probability (dhy.6)? The answer is a per-feature stop-probability table — the empirical seed of a routing cost model — and an honest "explained fraction".

## Depends on: dhy.10, dhy.6.

## Steps
1. Write `scripts/validate_stop_model.py` that joins `observed_stops_*.csv` (per-node passes/stops) with the OSM node classification from dhy.10. Classify every observed node into exactly one class, in this precedence: traffic_signals · stop · give_way · roundabout entry · level crossing · signalled crossing · inferred yield (minor meets major, per the dhy.10 rule) · equal-class uncontrolled junction · mid-way (no junction within 20 m). Acceptance: every node gets a class; counts per class in the note.
2. For each class report: nodes, passes, stops, stop probability with a 95 % Wilson interval. Use only nodes with ≥ 5 passes for the headline table; show the all-nodes table too. Acceptance: table with ≥ 5 classes populated (if Eric's data is thin, say which classes are under-powered rather than dropping them).
3. Compute the **explained fraction**: share of all observed stop events that occur at a node whose class is anything other than mid-way / equal-class uncontrolled. Also compute precision and recall of the binary rule "OSM says stop-cause present ⇒ cyclist stops on ≥ 50 % of passes". Acceptance: three numbers in the note.
4. Unexplained stops: list the top 15 nodes by stop count classified mid-way or equal-class uncontrolled. For each, inspect OSM (and Mapillary/Street View if available in a browser; otherwise OSM only) and label the cause manually: missing OSM tag · traffic queue · café/photo/regroup · descent hairpin · data noise. Acceptance: labelled table; share of "missing OSM tag" reported — that is the OSM completeness gap seen from the saddle.
5. Write `docs/research/stop-model-validation.md` following TEMPLATE.md. Verdict must answer: can a stop-cost model built from OSM features alone optimise for flow credibly (yes / yes-with-empirical-correction / no), and which classes carry the most weight.

## Edge cases
- If only OSM public traces (source B) are available, note that they are not road-cyclist-specific and widen the intervals accordingly; still produce the table.
- Node precedence matters where a junction has both signals and a give_way on a slip — signals win; say so.
- Stops caused by the ride starting/ending are already excluded upstream; do not re-filter.

## Done when
Note + script committed; per-class probability table, explained fraction, precision/recall and the labelled unexplained-stops table are all present.
notes: From dhy.6 review (2026-10-20): (1) passes/stops fragment across nodes a few metres apart (e.g. signalised crossing 6649584866 has 16 passes, neighbour 686757750 has 17) — group nodes within 15-20 m into one junction unit before computing stop probability; (2) a few OSM-trace rows have probability > 1 because stops are per event and passes per ride — cap stops at one per ride per node unit; (3) Ireland data is thin (311 slow stops, 90 nodes with >=5 passes and >=1 stop) — use the Berlin outputs from bike-mapper-dhy.15 as well (pause-event dominated, auto-pause on); (4) Ireland rides have auto-pause OFF so stops are slow-speed runs, Berlin rides have it ON so stops are timer gaps — treat both kinds as stops.

title: OSM stop-cause features: signals/stop/give-way/roundabout coverage, yield-inference rule, expected stops/km per way
description:
## Question
Which OSM features imply a forced stop for a cyclist, how completely are they mapped in the study region, and what does a first "expected stops per km" per way look like?

## Depends on: dhy.1 (scaffold), dhy.2 (Ireland extract + tag-coverage script conventions).

## Steps
1. Write `scripts/osm_stop_features.py` (pyosmium, two passes: nodes then ways) that counts, in the Ireland extract: nodes with `highway` ∈ {traffic_signals, stop, give_way, crossing, mini_roundabout, turning_circle}, `railway=level_crossing`, `traffic_calming=*`, `barrier=*` on road ways; ways with `junction=roundabout|circular`; and the directionality qualifiers `direction=*`, `stop:direction`, `traffic_signals:direction`, `crossing=*` (uncontrolled/traffic_signals/zebra). Output a markdown table of counts and the fraction of stop/give_way/traffic_signals nodes that carry a direction qualifier. Acceptance: table in the note; script runs < 10 min.
2. Junction detection: build the set of nodes shared by ≥ 2 distinct road-cycling highway ways (motorway excluded; include service only if `service` is unset). For each such node record the highest and lowest highway class meeting there. Report junction density (junctions per km) per highway class. Acceptance: table in the note.
3. Define and document the **yield-inference rule** for unsignalled, untagged junctions, since OSM rarely tags give_way per approach: a way yields where it meets a higher-class way (`unclassified` meeting `tertiary` → the unclassified approach stops; equal class → treat as 50 % unless `priority_road` says otherwise; `junction=roundabout` entry → yield). Write the rule as an ordered list with the class hierarchy spelled out. Acceptance: rule present with no undefined cases for the highway classes in step 1.
4. Compute a first **expected stops per km** per way = (signals + stops + give-ways + inferred yields + roundabout entries + crossings-with-signals) / way length, travelling in each direction. Dump per-way CSV to `data/samples/stops_per_km_wicklow.csv` for ways inside the Wicklow bbox (≈ 53.0–53.3 N, −6.5–−6.1 E; the same bbox other tasks use). Report: distribution per highway class (median, p90) and the 20 longest road stretches in the bbox with < 0.2 expected stops/km. Acceptance: CSV + two tables in the note.
5. Completeness check against an independent source: Dublin City Council publishes its traffic-signal site list (SCATS sites) on data.gov.ie / Smart Dublin. Download it, reproject to WGS84, and report what fraction of those sites have an OSM `highway=traffic_signals` node within 30 m (recall of OSM). Acceptance: recall number in the note with the dataset URL and licence; if the dataset cannot be found, record the search terms tried and use the OSM-vs-OSM proxy of `crossing=traffic_signals` without a nearby `highway=traffic_signals`.
6. Write `docs/research/osm-stop-features.md` following TEMPLATE.md. Verdict must say: which stop causes OSM captures well, which it misses, and whether an OSM-only stop estimate is credible enough to route on before empirical validation (dhy.11).

## Edge cases
- A `highway=traffic_signals` node on a one-way carriageway counts once; on a two-way way without a direction qualifier count for both directions and flag the assumption.
- Pedestrian `crossing` nodes without `crossing=traffic_signals` do not force a stop; count them separately, not in the estimate.
- Exclude `highway=traffic_signals` nodes that sit only on `footway`/`cycleway` ways from the road estimate.
- Keep the SCATS download out of git except a ≤ 1 MB sample.

## Done when
Note + script + CSV committed; the Wicklow "low-stop stretches" table and the Dublin recall number are present; yield-inference rule is explicit.

title: Routing engines: node-level stop costs and turn costs — comparison + hands-on BRouter 'flow' profile
description:
## Question
Which open-source routing engine can (1) do road-bike routing with a customisable cost profile, (2) apply **node-level costs** (traffic signals, stop, give-way, roundabout entry) and **turn costs** (right turns across traffic — Ireland drives on the left), (3) accept externally derived per-node/per-way stop probabilities, (4) return elevation-aware routes, and (5) run cheaply self-hosted for a one-country graph?

## Depends on: dhy.1, dhy.2 (extract), dhy.10 (stop-feature script, used to score routes).

## Steps
1. Comparison table in `docs/research/routing-engines.md` (TEMPLATE.md), rows: BRouter, GraphHopper (open-source core, custom-model JSON), Valhalla (dynamic costing), OSRM (Lua profiles); hosted options (openrouteservice, GraphHopper Directions API) for comparison only. Columns: licence · profile language · **node-tag costing** (how: BRouter `initialcost`/node context, GraphHopper custom-model limitations, Valhalla `traffic_signal_penalty`/`stop_penalty`, OSRM node function) · **turn costs** (left/right/u-turn, per-class) · injecting external per-node/per-way scores (tag injection pre-build vs runtime) · elevation · alternatives · round-trip · RAM/build time for Ireland · maturity. Acceptance: GPX produced.
3. Score any route for expected stops: write `scripts/score_route_stops.py` that snaps a GPX to OSM ways/nodes and sums stop-cause features along it using the dhy.10 classification (signals, stops, give-ways, inferred yields, roundabout entries) → stops per km, plus the count of right turns at junctions (Ireland: across traffic). Acceptance: prints the score for the baseline GPX.
4. Hands-on flow profile: copy `fastbike` to `profiles/flow.brf` and add heavy `initialcost` for `highway=traffic_signals|stop|give_way` nodes and roundabout entry, plus a turn-cost penalty for right turns at junctions if BRouter supports it (document if not). title: Empirical stop detection from ride GPS: Eric's Garmin/Strava export + OSM timestamped public traces
description:
## Question
Where do cyclists actually stop? Derive observed stop events from ride GPS and attach them to OSM nodes, so the OSM-based stop estimate (dhy.10) can be validated (dhy.11).

## Depends on: dhy.1, dhy.2.

## Data sources, in priority order
A. **Eric's own ride history** — Garmin Connect or Strava bulk export (FIT/GPX/TCX) dropped into `data/rides/` (gitignored). Personal data; usable without ToS concerns. **If `data/rides/` is empty when this task starts, do steps 3–6 on source B only, write the source-A section as "pending Eric's export", and say so in the summary — do not block.**
B. **OSM public GPS traces with timestamps** — `GET https://api.openstreetmap.org/api/0.6/trackpoints?bbox=…&page=N` for the Wicklow bbox; only traces uploaded as *identifiable* or *trackable* carry timestamps. Page until exhausted or 60 pages; polite User-Agent and ≥ 1 s delay. Save raw GPX under `data/gps/`.
C. Document but do not pull: Strava API v3 activity streams (`velocity_smooth`, `moving`) for one's own activities — note the rate limits and that the API agreement forbids using *other users'* data to build routing products (cite the clause and URL). Ride with GPS / Komoot export formats, one line each.

## Steps
1. Write `scripts/stop_events.py` that parses FIT (via `fitparse` or `fitdecode` — add to pyproject), GPX and TCX into a uniform (timestamp, lat, lon, speed-if-present) stream. Acceptance: runs on a sample of each format (make a tiny synthetic GPX if no real one exists).
2. Define a **stop event** precisely and write the definition into the note: speed < 1.0 m/s (computed from consecutive points if not recorded) sustained ≥ 3 s; merge events < 10 s apart; discard events within 200 m of ride start/end; treat recording gaps > 30 s as auto-pause stops (count separately, since Garmin auto-pause hides the stop duration). Acceptance: definition in the note; parameters are CLI flags with these defaults.
3. Snap each stop event and each ride trackpoint to the nearest OSM node/way within 20 m (STRtree over the Ireland extract's road nodes/ways; reuse the snap helper from earlier scripts if one exists, else write `scripts/snap.py` once and reuse it). Acceptance: snap rate (% of points matched) in the note.
4. Compute **per-node stop probability** = stop events at node / passes through node (a pass = the ride trajectory traverses the node without a stop or with one), and **per-way observed stops per km** per direction. Write `data/samples/observed_stops_<source>.csv` (node id, lat, lon, passes, stops, probability). Acceptance: CSV present; nodes with ≥ 5 passes highlighted.
5. Report for each source: number of rides/traces, total km, fraction of traces with timestamps (source B), stop events found, top 20 nodes by stop count with ≥ 5 passes. Acceptance: tables in the note.
6. Write `docs/research/empirical-stops.md` following TEMPLATE.md. Verdict must answer: (a) is Eric's own history large enough to validate a stop model (give km and node-with-≥5-passes count); (b) is OSM timestamped trace density in Ireland enough to serve as a public substitute (numbers); (c) which non-personal source is the realistic best option.

## Edge cases
- Speed from Garmin may be absent in GPX exports; compute from haversine distance / Δt and smooth over 3 points.
- Traffic-light stops in a group ride cluster at the same node; passes must be counted per ride, not per point.
- OSM traces include cars and walkers; report the fraction of trackpoints on `motorway`/`trunk` and with median speed > 12 m/s as contamination, and exclude those traces from the stop statistics.
- Never commit `data/rides/` or raw GPS; only the aggregated CSVs.

Note + scripts + CSVs committed; (a)(b)(c) answered; if source A was absent, the note says so explicitly and the task still closes.

title: Carriageway width per OSM way from Tailte Eireann HVD Ways polygons (CC BY 4.0) for Dublin/Wicklow
description:
Why: docs/research/road-cycle-open-data-ireland.md found the open Tailte Eireann High Value Dataset 'Ways' feature service (services-eu1.arcgis.com/FH5XCsx8rYXqnjF5/arcgis/rest/services/Ways/FeatureServer/9; CC BY 4.0; 618,183 carriageway polygons nationally, fields GUID/OBJECTID/Shape only). OSM width covers 0.5% of Irish road km; a measured carriageway width would feed a pinch/overtaking cost and a road-vs-lane width check. Sample: data/opendata/tailte_ways/ways_rathmines_ranelagh.geojson (1,284 polygons).
Steps:
1. scripts/tailte_ways_fetch.py: page the REST query (resultOffset, 2,000 per page, outSR=4326, f=geojson) for a bbox argument into data/opendata/tailte_ways/<bbox>.geojson; start with the planner bbox -6.6,52.95,-6.0,53.4; log pages and feature count; respect a 0.5 s delay between pages.
2. scripts/tailte_width.py: for each OSM road way (highway in build_cycle_overlay.ROAD_HW) in the bbox, sample points every 25 m along the way, find the containing polygon, measure width as 2 x distance from the point to the polygon boundary (shapely, EPSG:2157); write per-way median/p10/p90 width to data/samples/osm_way_width_tailte_<area>.csv (< 1 MB; subset if needed).
3. Validate on 20 ways with OSM width or lanes tags and 5 ways Eric knows (Rathmines Road, Dundrum Road, Military Road, Sally Gap R759, Rathfarnham Road): table of measured vs expected; write docs/research/tailte-ways-width.md per TEMPLATE.md with verdict.
Acceptance: fetch is resumable; width CSV produced for the planner bbox; validation table with error in metres; attribution '(c) Tailte Eireann, CC BY 4.0' recorded in the note; pytest/ruff unaffected.
Ambiguity: polygons may cover footways or verges in places (description says 'skin of the earth'); report the fraction of sample points not inside any polygon and inspect 10 of them before trusting widths.

title: Evaluate NTA 2013 GDA Cycle Network Survey (per-direction pavement quality, junction delay, QoS) as priors for the flow model
description:
Why: docs/research/road-cycle-open-data-ireland.md found data/opendata/nta_cycnet_2013/CycNet/CycleNetwork_GDA.shp (CC-BY 4.0, 7,234 polylines, surveyed 2011-2012, Navteq-linked) with per-direction fields WD_/AD_ PvmtQua (1-5), Width (1-5), NumConf, JuncDel (1/3/5), Comfort (1-5), Gradien, QoS (A+..D), Char (C1/C2/C3/B1/G1/S1/S2). It is the only open per-segment pavement-quality and junction-delay source for Dublin; OSM smoothness covers 5% of Dublin road km.
Steps:
1. scripts/nta2013_match.py: read the shapefile with pyshp (uv run --with pyshp) or add pyshp to the project; reproject ITM->WGS84; match each link to OSM ways (data/osm/ireland.osm.pbf, bbox -6.45,53.25,-6.05,53.45) by buffer 15 m + heading; emit data/samples/nta2013_osm_match.csv (osm_way, nta link id, direction, PvmtQua, JuncDel, Comfort, QoS).
2. Correlate: (a) PvmtQua vs OSM surface/smoothness where both exist (contingency table); (b) JuncDel vs the planner's expected stops/km per way (data/osm/stops_per_km_* or the event model) and vs empirical stops where Eric's rides cover the links (data/samples/observed_ways_eric.csv).
3. Report Spearman correlations and a 2x2 of 'JuncDel=5' vs 'stops/km above median'; write docs/research/nta-2013-survey-priors.md per TEMPLATE.md with a usable / not usable verdict on using PvmtQua as a weak surface prior and JuncDel as a stop prior.
Acceptance: match rate reported (links matched / 7,234); correlations with n; note added to docs/research/README.md; pytest/ruff unaffected.
Ambiguity: the survey predates most post-2019 schemes; restrict the stop correlation to links whose Char is unchanged in the NTA 2025 layer, and say how that was decided.

title: Cycle overlay QA diff: NTA 2025 cycle infrastructure vs OSM lanes/tracks (Dublin)
description:
Why: docs/research/road-cycle-open-data-ireland.md found the NTA 'Dublin Metropolitan Area Cycle Infrastructure 2025' layer (CC-BY 4.0, 4,410 features, 975.7 side-km; fields BIKE in {BIKE_LANE, SEPARATE_TRAIL, BIKE_FRIENDLY_PEDESTRIAN_PATH, NON_TRAFFIC_TRAIL, SHARED_ROAD}, DIR in {Forward, Bi-Directional, Reverse}) agrees with the OSM overlay within 2% in Rathmines-Ranelagh, so its value is as a diff that finds OSM omissions, not as a routing input.
Steps:
1. scripts/nta_osm_cycle_diff.py: load data/opendata/nta_cycle_2025/nta_cycle_network_2025.geojson (download URL in the note) and web/data/cycle_dublin_wicklow.geojson (or the OSM PBF via build_cycle_overlay.classify); project both to EPSG:2157; for each NTA feature find OSM road/cycleway ways within 15 m with heading within 30 deg; side-aware match (NTA Forward = one side; OSM side left/right/both).
2. Classify each NTA segment as matched / OSM-missing (NTA BIKE_LANE or SEPARATE_TRAIL with no OSM lane/track/cycleway nearby) and each OSM lane/track way as NTA-missing; write web/data/cycle_diff_dublin.geojson (< 2 MB, Douglas-Peucker 1.5e-5) with props kind, nta_class, osm_kind, reason.
3. Print km and counts per disagreement class to stderr; save a summary to data/samples/nta_osm_cycle_diff_summary.md.
4. Add a toggleable 'NTA vs OSM diff' layer to the planner map next to the cycle overlay (web/ UI), styled distinctly; keep existing tests green and add one unit test for the matcher on 3 synthetic cases.
Acceptance: script runs in < 2 min; summary table in data/samples; diff layer visible in the planner; attribution 'Contains NTA data, CC-BY 4.0' in the layer legend.
Ambiguity: NTA draws both sides as separate Forward features; decide and document how a 'both' OSM way is matched to two NTA features.

title: flowplan.scoring follow-ups: dist_along_km to node not segment end; no-from-node fallback; --snap-m CLI flags; tests for cos filter and per-segment dedup
description: Reviewer minors from emq.3 (scripts/flowplan/scoring.py): (1) hits[].dist_along_km is measured to the end of the matched segment, not to the node's projection on it; BRouter omits collinear points so this can be off by hundreds of metres - project the node onto the segment and add that fraction. (2) Index rows with an empty from-node can never match (lines ~140-143); implement the bead-3 rule (node-only match when no other event at that node matched) and add a test; the Ireland index has 0 such rows today so there is no behaviour change. (3) scripts/flow_score.py: add --snap-m and --node-snap-m so a GPS track can be scored with a wider radius; document in the docstring that node_snap_m=1.0 assumes BRouter output. (4) Add unit tests for the arrival-edge cosine >= 0.5 filter, the one-arrival-per-node-per-segment rule, and the previous-segment skip (including a loop route that revisits a node later and must count it twice). title: Classify OSM signal nodes in Dublin as junction vs standalone crossing using DCC/SDCC/DLR signal-site lists
description:
Why: docs/research/stop-priors-open-data.md (emq.11) found that ~45% of Dublin signal sites are standalone pedestrian crossings (DCC 348/850 typed Pedestrian/Pelican, SDCC 213/375) which rest on green and stop a cyclist far less often than a SCATS junction (prior 0.06 vs 0.40). OSM tagging (highway=traffic_signals vs crossing=traffic_signals) is not reliable enough on its own for that split.
Inputs (CC-BY 4.0, already in data/samples/): dcc_traffic_signal_sites_151025.csv (Site Number, Site Name, Latitude, Longitude, Type), sdcc_signalised_junctions_crossings.csv (ITM X/Y, Type), dlr_scats_sites.csv (no type; Site_ID, Location, Lat, Long).
Steps: 1. Load the three lists, reproject SDCC ITM (EPSG:2157) to WGS84. 2. For each OSM signal-class event node in the Ireland flow index within the DCC/SDCC/DLR areas, find the nearest authority site within 30 m; assign class xing_signal if Type is Pedestrian/Pelican/Pedestrian Crossing, signal if Junction, keep the OSM class otherwise. 3. Report counts: matched/unmatched, class changes, and the distance distribution. 4. Unit test on a handful of known sites (e.g. DCC site 1 Abbey St @ Marlborough St = Junction (Luas)).
Done when: a script or build_flow_index step applies the override behind a flag, counts are in the note or a data/samples/ CSV, and pytest passes. Ambiguity: whether to also trust the DLR list (no type) only as a 'this is a signal' confirmation.
