title: Surface quality beyond OSM: Mapillary density and Irish PSCI pavement data
description:
## Question
Beyond OSM's `surface`/`smoothness` tags (coverage measured in the OSM note), what open sources could tell a road cyclist how rough a road is — the "road feel" reading of flow?

## Depends on: OSM road-network note (reuse its coverage numbers; do not recompute).

## Steps
1. Inventory in `docs/research/surface-quality.md` (TEMPLATE.md): Mapillary (API v4, CC BY-SA imagery, coverage density; whether map-feature detections include road-surface classes), KartaView/OpenStreetCam, national pavement-condition surveys (TII Pavement Condition / PSCI ratings for Irish local roads — the Pavement Surface Condition Index is published by local authorities; UK DfT road condition statistics), and OSM Notes/StreetComplete as crowd-correction channels. Columns: licence, granularity, coverage in Ireland, access method, allowed-in-own-app. Acceptance: table complete.
2. Hands-on: query the Mapillary API for image counts in the same Wicklow bbox used by the cyclist-flow task and report images per km of `tertiary`+`unclassified` road (snap image coordinates to nearest way within 15 m). Needs a free Mapillary client token — document how to obtain it and read it from `MAPILLARY_TOKEN` env var; never commit it. Acceptance: table in note; script `scripts/mapillary_density.py` committed.
3. Hands-on: find and download the PSCI dataset for at least one Irish county (search data.gov.ie for "PSCI" / "pavement surface condition"). Report: format, whether it is geo-referenced per road segment, rating scale, year. If not findable as open data, record the search terms tried and the closest thing found. Acceptance: either sample in `data/samples/` or a documented negative result.
4. Verdict: rank the three best signals for surface quality by (coverage × reliability × licence-friendliness) and say whether any is good enough to flag "avoid: rough surface" on minor Irish roads.

## Edge cases
- Mapillary rate limits: batch bbox queries into ≤0.05° tiles and back off on 429.
- PSCI ratings are per local-authority road segment IDs that may not map to OSM ways; note the join problem, do not solve it.

## Done when
Note + script + sample or negative result committed; verdict ranks the signals.
close_reason: Descoped after clarification: 'flow' means few forced stops, not surface roughness. Reopen if surface becomes a goal.

title: Motor-traffic flow: open AADT sources and their coverage of minor roads (TII, DfT)
description:
## Question
Is open motor-traffic volume data (AADT or similar) available at enough spatial density to classify the minor roads a road cyclist uses as quiet vs busy? This is one of the two readings of "flow data" and the hardest open-data gap for cycling planners.

## Steps
1. Inventory sources in `docs/research/motor-traffic-flow.md` (TEMPLATE.md): Ireland — TII Traffic Data (nra.ie/tii traffic counters, data.gov.ie), local-authority counters (Dublin City Council, Cork, Kildare etc. via data.gov.ie / Smart Dublin), NTA; UK — DfT Road Traffic Statistics (road-level AADF by count point), DfI Northern Ireland; EU spot-check — one continental source (e.g. French `Trafic moyen journalier annuel` on data.gouv.fr, or Spain's DGT/Mapa de Tráfico). Also OSM tags that proxy traffic (`traffic_volume`, `maxspeed`, `lanes`, highway class). Columns: licence, format, update frequency, number of count points, which road classes are covered, access method. Acceptance: table complete; state explicitly for each whether the licence permits reuse in an app.
2. Download the TII (Ireland) count-point dataset and the DfT GB AADF count-point CSV into `data/traffic/`. Acceptance: files present; row counts logged.
3. Write `scripts/traffic_coverage.py` that loads the count points, snaps each to the nearest OSM highway way within 30 m (use the OSM extract + a spatial index; shapely STRtree is fine), and reports the number of count points per highway class. Then report what fraction of total km of `tertiary` + `unclassified` road lies within 2 km of any count point. Acceptance: two tables in the note for Ireland; same for one GB region if the full-GB run is too slow (say which region).
4. Record the verdict honestly: in most countries counts exist only on national/regional roads. State what % of road-cyclist-relevant road km has no count within 2 km, and whether that makes direct AADT use (a) a full layer, (b) a training signal for an estimator, or (c) useless.
5. List at least three proxy/derived approaches with one-line feasibility each: OSM highway class + maxspeed heuristic; population/POI gravity model; commercial feeds (TomTom/HERE traffic — note cost and licence); Mapillary image-based car counts. Acceptance: list present; no implementation.

## Edge cases
- Count points often sit on dual carriageways; the 30 m snap may pick the wrong carriageway — note the limitation, do not fix it.
- CRS: TII may publish in Irish Grid (EPSG:29902) or ITM (EPSG:2157); DfT in OSGB (EPSG:27700). Reproject to WGS84 before snapping; assert the reprojected points fall inside the country bbox.
- If TII data requires a manual portal download, document the exact clicks and commit a small sample to `data/samples/` with its licence.

## Done when
Note + script + samples committed; the "within 2 km" coverage number for Irish tertiary+unclassified roads is in the note and the verdict picks (a)/(b)/(c).

title: Elevation: compare open DEMs and measure profile accuracy on a known Irish climb
description:
## Question
Which open elevation model is good enough for ClimbFinder-grade gradient profiles (per-100 m gradient, climb categorisation) in the study region, and how is it accessed?

## Steps
1. Build a comparison table in `docs/research/elevation.md` (TEMPLATE.md format) covering at minimum: Copernicus GLO-30, SRTM 1-arcsec, EU-DEM v1.1, Tailte Éireann / OSi open DTM products (check data.gov.ie and tailte.ie for any open 2 m–10 m DTM), OPW LiDAR, and the UK Environment Agency LiDAR (for the Northern Ireland boundary case). Columns: resolution, vertical accuracy (as published), licence, coverage, access method (URL/API/bulk), file format, cost. Acceptance: every row has every column filled or an explicit "not published".
2. Download one tile from Copernicus GLO-30 covering a known Irish climb (suggested: Sally Gap / Wicklow Gap, Co. Wicklow; or Conor Pass, Co. Kerry) into `data/dem/`. If OSi/Tailte open DTM exists, download the matching tile too. Acceptance: tiles present, sizes logged.
3. Write `scripts/elevation_profile.py` that takes a GPX file (or a lat/lon polyline) and a DEM GeoTIFF, samples elevation every 25 m along the line (bilinear), and prints: total ascent, max gradient over 100 m windows, and a CSV of distance/elevation/gradient. Acceptance: runs on a hand-made GPX of the chosen climb (trace it from OSM way geometry via Overpass or draw 10–20 points) and prints plausible numbers (Conor Pass ≈ 400 m ascent from Dingle side; Wicklow Gap ≈ 300 m from Laragh).
4. Compare against a reference: published climb stats from ClimbFinder/Quäldich/Wikipedia for the same climb (record the URL). Report the difference in total ascent and max gradient per DEM. Acceptance: comparison table present; note any voids/no-data cells hit.
5. Record the elevation-service alternatives (Open-Elevation, OpenTopoData, Mapbox/Google terrain APIs) with licence and rate limits in the Sources table, as a hosted-vs-self-hosted option.

## Edge cases
- GLO-30 uses EGM2008 geoid heights; SRTM uses EGM96 — note it, it does not matter for gradients but matters for absolute elevation comparisons.
- Bilinear sampling near no-data cells must not produce NaN silently; log and skip.
- Keep downloaded tiles out of git; put only the small CSV output in `data/samples/`.

## Done when
Note + script + sample CSV committed; verdict names the recommended DEM for Ireland and the fallback for the rest of Europe, with the measured error from step 4.
